column1: # The YANC instruction set: one row per mnemonic, and the source of truth that
# Scripts/check_isa.py holds the hand-written copies to. The ISA is spelled out
# in four places that nothing keeps in step -- ASMComp.l (mnemonic -> opcode +
# operand class), instr_dec.v and ula.v (opcode -> control signals and ALU
# operation) and core.v (which hard-codes the flow-control opcodes as 5-bit
# literals) -- and a disagreement between them is silent: a program assembles
# and then runs as a different program. TODO.md item 10.2.
#          data    an address in data memory
#          code    an address in instruction memory
#          offset  a data address plus a constant offset (array access)
#          lea     the ADDRESS of a data name, as a constant (pseudo-op)
# acc:     what it does to the accumulator -- r, w, rw or -
# stack:   push, pop or -   (one word of the data stack)
# opnd:    what it does to the data word the operand NAMES --
#          base_r  reads an unknown word of the array it names (indirect)
#          base_w  writes an unknown word of the array it names (indirect)
#          addr    takes its address only; the value is not touched
# flow:    jmp, jz, call, ret or -
# Several mnemonics share one opcode and differ only in how the assembler reads
# the operand: LOD, LEA and LOD_V are all opcode 0.
# WHERE THE EFFECT COLUMNS COME FROM, and how far to trust them. They are
# derived from the naming convention the ISA follows without exception --
# prefix P_/PF_ pushes the accumulator first, prefix S_/SF_ takes the second
# operand off the stack, suffix _M reads the operand from memory instead of the
# accumulator, suffix _V adds a constant offset -- plus the per-mnemonic
# comments in ASMComp.l, which is where LDA, STA, LEA and the indirect forms
# come from. check_isa.py re-derives them from the names and fails on any row
# that breaks the convention, so a typo cannot survive here. What that does NOT
# give is execution: no instruction has been run to confirm its effect. The
# instruction-set simulator of TODO item 10.1 is what will validate these
# columns; until it exists they are a careful reading, not a measurement.
